content: The Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Prevention, Testing, Treatment, Service Delivery, and Monitoring: Recommendations for a Public Health Approach were updated in July 2021 by the World Health Organization (WHO). These guidelines build upon the 2016 edition titled Consolidated Guidelines on the Use of Antiretroviral Drugs for Treating and Preventing HIV Infection: Recommendations for a Public Health Approach, 2nd Edition. The updated guidelines incorporate advancements and evidence-based practices in HIV care and prevention that have emerged between 2016 and 2021. The publication is available in both electronic (ISBN 978-92-4-003159-3) and print (ISBN 978-92-4-003160-9) formats. WHO permits the non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution of this work, provided proper citation is given. The guidelines aim to provide comprehensive recommendations for the diagnosis, prevention, treatment, and care of HIV, structured along the continuum of HIV services. They emphasize a person-centered approach to care, ensuring equitable access to high-quality services regardless of geographic or economic disparities. The guidelines also align with the UNAIDS 2025 targets, which aim for 95% of people living with HIV to know their status, 95% of those diagnosed to initiate treatment, and 95% of those on treatment to achieve viral suppression. These targets also focus on removing societal and legal barriers to accessing services and integrating HIV responses into broader efforts to achieve universal health coverage as part of the Sustainable Development Goals. Significant developments in HIV care since 2016 include the introduction of dolutegravir, self-testing, expanded viral load and infant testing, new options for tuberculosis (TB) preventive therapy, and post-exposure prophylaxis. Advanced HIV disease remains a challenge in reducing mortality, but differentiated service delivery models have shown promise in improving care quality. New point-of-care viral load testing technologies offer additional opportunities to enhance service delivery. In prevention, clinical trials have confirmed the efficacy of antiretroviral drugs like tenofovir in reducing HIV transmission. The guidelines also highlight the importance of community-based approaches to diagnosis, prevention, and treatment, empowering individuals and communities to manage their health effectively. By supporting people living with HIV and their communities, the global health community can work towards ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. The guidelines were developed with contributions from numerous experts, organizations, and WHO departments. External peer reviewers and contributors provided critical input, ensuring the guidelines reflect the latest scientific evidence and best practices. WHO staff and consultants coordinated the consolidation process, with technical leads and reviewers contributing to specific chapters. The guidelines also acknowledge the voluntary contributions of experts in palliative care and drug-drug interactions.
